speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a country and as a Government, we do not condone or tolerate corruption.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Domestically, corruption cases are investigated by the Corrupt Practices Investigations Bureau (CPIB).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Thereafter, cases are assessed by the Public Prosecutor, who acts independently.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Internationally, we know that there are many places in the world where corruption is endemic and the business environment is very different from Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore companies have to operate in all kinds of environments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But as a matter of principle, we expect that they must do so while keeping their systems clean and complying with the laws of the countries where they operate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They must develop ways of operating which enable them to do this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They cannot lower their own standards of integrity and they must not bring back to Singapore practices alien to the norms which we have established with such great effort here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: How we handle allegations of corrupt acts overseas by Singaporeans or Singapore companies depends on a number of factors, including (a) whether the case is connected more strongly to Singapore or to other countries; (b) any practical or legal difficulty in investigating the case, bearing in mind that the evidence will mainly be overseas; (c) any actions being taken by third countries and the legal and regulatory tools they are bringing to bear; and (d) any cooperative mechanisms between Singapore and the other countries involved.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In handling the Keppel Offshore and Marine (KOM) case, the authorities in the United States (US), Singapore and Brazil worked with one another and reached an agreed approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was no "three-nation plea bargain agreement", as Ms Sylvia Lim puts it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What happened was that each jurisdiction acted under its own domestic laws, but in coordination with the other two jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the US, the Department of Justice (DOJ) entered into a deferred prosecution agreement (DPA) with KOM.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is an agreement under US law, between KOM and DOJ.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amount was determined in accordance with US sentencing guidelines.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: DPA, which has been published, sets out how the amount was arrived at.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Among other things, KOM was given maximum credit for its full cooperation with investigations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The last 12.5% is payable to Singapore, but subject to any further penalties the Brazilian authorities may impose.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Brazil, the Federal Public Ministry entered into a leniency agreement on similar terms to the US DPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Singapore, the Public Prosecutor directed CPIB to administer a conditional warning on KOM.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In reaching this decision, the Public Prosecutor considered the following factors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, that KOM had voluntarily reported its internal findings to CPIB and the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) in September 2016 and had cooperated with all three jurisdictions in the investigation and resolution process, that KOM also indicated that it will voluntarily agree to the US DPA and the Brazilian leniency agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that the key elements of this case, in particular, the recipients of the bribes and the projects connected with the bribes, occurred outside Singapore, and the jurisdictions concerned are also acting against KOM, in coordination with Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A conditional warning allows Singapore to impose on KOM conditions that are closely aligned with the terms of the US DPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If any of the conditions are breached, KOM can be prosecuted.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The aligned approach results in a robust resolution to KOM's case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The trilateral resolution requires KOM to pay a total of US$422 million.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If KOM fails to pay the penalty, there will be consequences under the US, Singapore and Brazilian law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Any penalty or claim that KOM might be subject to under Singapore law would be far less than what KOM is now liable for under the coordinated resolution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Furthermore, KOM is also required under the US DPA to strengthen its internal controls and compliance and anti-corruption programmes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The current resolution, therefore, achieves more than what we would have been able to do if we had proceeded against the company solely under the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Png Eng Huat asked about the action to be taken against the individuals concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As AGC has stated, investigations into the individuals concerned are ongoing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Singapore investigations are conducted on the same timeframe as the US and Brazilian investigations and go back to 2001, when the corrupt acts first took place.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is no agreement, whether in the DPA or otherwise, which prevents the disclosure of the individuals under investigation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, for criminal investigations, it is standard practice in Singapore, and in many other jurisdictions, not to identify individuals under investigation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is for the simple reason that investigations can lead to the conclusion that no offence is made out, or that prosecution is unwarranted, in which case disclosure would have been prejudicial to the individuals concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Individuals will be identified if and when charges are preferred in Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The case involves many projects in Brazil and goes back many years to 2001.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Most of the evidence, including documents and witnesses, are located in different jurisdictions, including Brazil and the US.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Legal proceedings have also taken place in these jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGC needs evidence from these jurisdictions, and it has sought assistance, and it is continuing to work with foreign authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGC has asked for certain information from them and some of its requests are still pending.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGC anticipates that further requests will have to be made as the investigations develop.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is a procedure whereby one country formally seeks assistance from another to obtain or secure evidence for use in its own investigations and proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This request will be reviewed and administered by the courts of the foreign country.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: How quickly and to what extent these requests and applications will be processed is a matter for the jurisdiction to which the request is made.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Likewise, any incoming requests from foreign jurisdictions would also have to be considered and acted upon.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Obviously, the intention is to move as expeditiously as possible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, as I have explained, not all aspects of the investigation are within our control.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Only after the investigations are completed can the AGC properly assess the case and decide on the appropriate response.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is something for the Public Prosecutor to decide, independently.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: How the Public Prosecutor decides will depend on several factors, including the culpability of each individual, the available evidence and what is appropriate in the circumstances.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, it will be important to determine, for each individual, what he knew, the extent of his involvement, his motivations, any personal benefit he obtained, the circumstances under which the relevant acts took place and any cooperation rendered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked for statistics on concluded or ongoing investigations into corrupt practices by Government-linked companies (GLCs) by overseas and local authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I cannot speak for what foreign jurisdictions may be doing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Insofar as Singapore is concerned, past investigations which have resulted in prosecutions are a matter of public record.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not comment on ongoing investigations, if any, for good reason: so as not to jeopardise the investigations or prejudice individuals or companies if it turns out that no offence is disclosed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Suffice to say, if there is good reason to investigate, the authorities will do so, whether or not the company is a GLC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government's relationship with Temasek Holdings is that of a shareholder.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government does not interfere in, nor influence the business decisions or operations of Temasek and its portfolio companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Likewise, Temasek does not interfere in the business decisions or operations of its portfolio companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are the responsibilities of the respective companies' boards and management.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Temasek holds the boards of its portfolio companies responsible for running the companies honestly and competently.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the boards do not perform, Temasek can, collectively with the other shareholders, change the board.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To reiterate, the Government expects all Singapore companies, their officers and their employees to comply fully with the laws of Singapore and the laws of the jurisdictions in which they operate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have to find ways to keep their own systems clean even when doing business in complex and challenging environments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Above all, they must not import corrupt practices into Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, I have four supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in her response, the Senior Minister of State mentioned that I was not correct to categorise the arrangements reached between Keppel and the Singapore authorities as a three-nation plea bargain agreement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What we read, however, from the statement by CPIB and AGC in December, is that this DPA in the US was reached, of course, with the US government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But in discussion with Brazil and Singapore, and as part of that global resolution, Singapore was issuing a conditional warning to KOM here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, my question is: is the Senior Minister of State actually saying that these agreements that we have reached with Keppel for the conditional warning were not taken in consultation or as part of arrangements with the US and Brazil, which seems to be what the statement is implying, and that we reached it independently, and we could have actually gone on to prosecute KOM if we had wanted to, it would not be in breach of any global arrangement?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, that is the first question, whether we are completely free to decide whether to prosecute or not in these discussions with Brazil and the US.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second question is that the Senior Minister of State mentioned in her response that the conditional warning, of course, carried certain undertakings from KOM which were closely aligned with the undertakings in the US agreement, but she did not really specify whether they were coterminous or whether there were variations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like the Senior Minister of State to give some examples of some of the key undertakings that we have included in the Singapore agreement with KOM.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The third question is, in the Senior Minister of State's response, she mentioned that by reaching this arrangement, we would have achieved much more than we could have on our own.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The CPIB and AGC statement says that KOM is being given a conditional warning in lieu of prosecution under PCA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure whether the Senior Minister of State, in her response, was actually saying that it would have been quite difficult to successfully prosecute KOM, because the evidence was overseas and so on and so forth, in which case, then it is a question of whether this "in lieu of prosecution" really means anything.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Looking at what has been happening to Keppel as a GLC, as a corporate entity, given the large sums of money involved and the damage to our reputation, people perceive that they are just being given a slap on the wrist, whereas it is a daily affair that individuals who are not well connected, they are prosecuted for corruption offences involving $10 or $20 and they go to jail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like the Government to respond to that because I think there is some public concern about this, what is perceived to be some lenient treatment being given to KOM.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Her first question was whether I had, in my reply, suggested that the actions taken by the AGC were not done in consultation or coordination with the other authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I said that there was no "three-nation plea bargain agreement".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What I was trying to explain is the legal basis or the legal concept behind it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Because when you say "three-nation plea bargain agreement", it suggests that there is either some kind of agreement or treaty to which all three countries are a party to and we are acting under the same instrument.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is what I said in the main reply and the intent of it was to explain the underlying basis, which is, that each country is actually acting in accordance with its own domestic laws.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is why in the US, they are acting under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and they are using the DPA mechanism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Singapore, we use the conditional warning and PCA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, of course, in Brazil, they had the Leniency Agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that was all that was being said in relation to that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second question was in reference to the main answer where I said that the terms of the conditional warning were closely aligned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, conditional warnings are things which had been given in the past by the agencies but, as a general practice, we do not disclose their exact terms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The third question was whether, when I said that we have achieved more than if we were acting on our own, and acting in lieu of prosecution, if I could just clarify with Ms Sylvia Lim her third question, what was the purport of that?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Yes, what I was asking was that the Senior Minister of State has said that some of the considerations in such transactions which take place primarily overseas and whether we decide to prosecute locally is, for example, whether our local authorities might have difficulties getting the evidence or witnesses locally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That is what I understood the Senior Minister of State to have said.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, my question was that when CPIB and AGC said in their statement that they are giving a warning in lieu of prosecution, is it a real risk of prosecution or is it a case where there will be difficulties and that is why we are saying that we are not prosecuting them but, in reality, the case would be difficult to mount?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this particular case, since Keppel has actually come forward and cooperated, it has, in effect, as a company, admitted its part in this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the point I was making, when I talked about being able to achieve more than we otherwise would have been able to do if we had proceeded solely ourselves, is for a number of reasons.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the maximum fine under PCA is $100,000 per charge.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this would not get us anywhere near the penalty under the global resolution or even Singapore's share of the current penalty.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And with respect to disgorgement, there will be issues of which country gets what.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, under the global resolution, what it means, essentially, is that we are able to achieve all the things that we would have been able to do with prosecution, but even more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And, in addition, under the US DPA, there are requirements for an enhanced compliance programme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, all of these are things which we have obtained, which is more than what we would have been able to obtain if you had proceeded solely under DPA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For this, I think it is important to understand that there are actually two different things.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, there is a company; second, there is the individual.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Insofar as the company is concerned, it is not a light thing at all.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is something like eight times whatever they would have paid out.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have been subject to an enhanced compliance regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I have pointed out, we have actually achieved more than what we would have been able to do if they were prosecuted solely under PCA and the company itself has obviously taken remedial actions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, as far as the company is concerned, make no mistake.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There has been a heavy price to pay and deservedly so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nobody has got off or not got off, as the case may be.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is something that the Public Prosecutor has to decide, and I have explained some of the challenges that the Public Prosecutor is facing in terms of getting the evidence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But that is something we have to let the Public Prosecutor deal with independently.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But let me just say one other thing on this, which is that it is not a matter of letting individuals off lightly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have, in the past, taken actions against people irrespective of their status.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the ST Marine case that I mentioned, all seven individuals were senior management, including former Presidents of ST Marine.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was Patrick Lee, the former Group Financial Controller of ST Marine; there was Ong Teck Liang, former Group Financial Controller; Han Yew Kwang, former Chief Operating Officer; Mok Kim Whang, former Senior Vice President; Tan Mong Seng, former President (Commercial Business), ST Marine; Chang Cheow Teck, former President, ST Marine; See Leong Teck, former President, ST Marine.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Government officials and politicians have been investigated in the past by CPIB and charged.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include the Minister of State Wee Toon Boon, sitting and former Members of Parliament Phey Yew Kok and Choo Wee Khiang, the Singapore Civil Defence Force Commissioner Peter Lim, National Kidney Foundation Chief Executive Officer (CEO) TT Durai, and the Deputy Chief Executive of the Public Utilities Board Choy Hon Tim.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As background, if a prominent company, especially one linked to the Government, fails to uphold the law and proper standards of conduct wherever they are, it hurts our national reputation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As my residents have told me, it is not enough just to win or get the job done.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My first question is: even if the Government or Temasek Holdings do not manage the day-to-day operations of GLCs, what measures are there to send a clear signal that Singaporeans and Singapore companies overseas must not engage in corrupt behaviour, whether directly or through proxy agents?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My second question is: does the Government have a view on whether KOM should conduct a claw-back of bonuses paid out to ex-employees implicated in illegal behaviour?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even if KOM has no legal means of claw-back, should such bonuses be subject to forfeit by law under the Penal Code or the PCA, if not so already?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, for Government tenders, what incentives are there to shape the behaviour of proxies and agents to minimise the risks of illegal activity?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, should there be punitive liquidated damages written into a tender in the event that a contractor is found to have breached the law either in Singapore or overseas?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I certainly agree that it does hurt our reputation and, for that reason, we do not condone this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are extremely disappointed as well in what has occurred.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the first question that the Member asked about what measures Temasek can take to send a clear signal to Singaporeans and Singapore companies, as I have said − and I repeat − the Government expects Singapore companies and Singaporeans to do business honestly and lawfully even in complex environments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For Temasek, their position is that they foster an ethos of integrity and good governance and sustainability, and they, too, do not condone improper conduct and malfeasance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, Temasek expects companies in its portfolio to abide by sound corporate governance and robust codes of conduct and ethics.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Temasek holds the respective boards and managements responsible and accountable for the day-to-day decisions and actions of these portfolio companies, but Temasek does not direct the day-to-day business decisions or operations of the Temasek portfolio companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But what Temasek can and does do is to conduct regular roundtables, forums, educational programmes, all essentially directed at encouraging not just its portfolio companies but all other companies to keep and maintain clean systems and avoid corrupt practices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second question the Member asked was about whether we have a view on whether KOM should claw back bonuses paid out to ex-employees and so on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government does not intervene in internal corporate disciplinary actions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The third supplementary question, I think, was with respect to tenders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Debarred entities will not be eligible to participate in any tender by Government agencies for a period of time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Beyond disbarment, the track record of a supplier is typically an evaluation criterion in Government tenders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first question is, in view of the Government's status as the largest single shareholder of Keppel, will Temasek Holdings call for an extraordinary general meeting with a view to pursue civil action against board members and senior executives found responsible for the bribery scheme for breach of fiduciary duties and to seek equitable compensation from those responsible?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to the questionable P-61 contract which amounted to hundreds of millions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would have likely required board approval for it to be approved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the Government aware whether the Keppel board gave the CEO broad powers to enter into the contract?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If not, what is the nature of the board's oversight and their culpability in the bribery scheme?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is this something the Public Prosecutor or CPIB is going to look into, or is this a matter for shareholders to consider?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, in its information release, the US DOJ shared that a KOM subsidiary in Singapore paid the bribes amounting to $17-odd million into an entity based in Miami, Florida.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And who are the officers of this subsidiary?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, a former Keppel CEO and Senior Adviser, Mr Choo Chiau Beng, was the Singapore Ambassador to Brazil from 2004 till 2016, I believe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Was Mr Choo removed as Ambassador because of his involvement or knowledge of the bribery scheme and, if so − and I stress, if so − which month or year did the Government first come to know of Mr Choo's involvement?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My final question pertains to the matter of the identities of the individuals identified in the DPA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is a dissonance between what the public reads in the newspapers for individuals who are being investigated, for example, the General Manager of Ang Mo Kio Town Council.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: No charges, I understand, have been preferred against him yet, but his identity, his name, is well-known to the public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How does the Minister reconcile that with the non-disclosure of the names of the individuals involved in the Keppel matter?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the Government's actions are that when investigations are ongoing, we do not disclose the identities of people being investigated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What other people may say outside, what other information may be floating outside, what other comments may go on in social media, that is separate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But as the Government, as an investigation authority, the Government does not disclose names of individuals who are being investigated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All civilised jurisdictions which observe the rule of law uphold that principle simply because, as I have mentioned earlier, we do not want to prejudice either the investigations or the persons being investigated, depending on how the investigation might turn out.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the first question, I think Mr Singh asked can the Government, as a shareholder, call a meeting and ask for a resolution to be passed to commence civil action.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think that was the thrust of the question.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Keppel Corporation then owns 100% of KOM, which is the entity in question here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the general principle of corporate governance, with which Mr Singh is familiar as a lawyer, is that the shareholders deal with their companies in which they have shares at the shareholder level.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The boards then, depending on whether the members are executive or non-executive, it is their business to make sure that the policies and so on for the company are proper, that governance is proper, and then the day-to-day operations are done by the executive team or the executive management.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I had mentioned earlier, in this particular instance, the Government and Temasek do not interfere in the day-to-day running or management of the Temasek portfolio companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have caused seven employees who participated in the conduct described in the statement of facts to separate from the company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have issued demotions and/or written warnings to seven employees who failed to detect the misconduct and failed to take appropriate steps to mitigate corruption and compliance risks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They have imposed approximately US$8.9 million in financial sanctions on 12 former or current employees as part of the disciplinary process and have conducted individualised anti-corruption and compliance training for six employees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Anything further than that is a matter for the Keppel group, or for the company in this case, to determine, not for the Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Going back to a couple of other questions asked by Mr Pritam Singh, on the P-61 contract, he asked whether—I am sorry, could the Member clarify his question on the P-61 contract?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Senior Minister of State said that the question really pertained to the nature of the board's oversight over that contract.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If, indeed, they had knowledge or they were involved in that contract, what was the nature of their oversight and their culpability in the bribery scheme and, specifically, is this something that CPIB or the Public Prosecutor is looking into?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is actually not so much a question for the Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As to what is known and not known within the Keppel group, that is, really, a Keppel matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The only thing that I can do here which would be useful is to point Mr Pritam Singh to one of Keppel's media releases, where Keppel said that the current boards of directors of Keppel Corporation and its unit KOM were not aware of the illegal payments made to secure projects in Brazil.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As far as the Government is concerned, as I have explained, the Government is a shareholder in Temasek, Temasek has a just over 20% shareholding in Keppel Corporation and the operations of Keppel are run by Keppel itself.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Pritam Singh also had a question on the name of the subsidiary company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not have that information with me.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And he asked about the circumstances in which Mr Choo Chiau Beng may have stepped down as ambassador, I do not have that information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What I can say is that he has stepped down and he is not involved in an ambassadorial role at the present time.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The Senior Minister of State is beginning to repeat herself in her answers.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And so, I will allow two supplementary questions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There will be no impact on the Government's fiscal position.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Temasek's 20% stake in KOM is just one part of its portfolio.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government's spending limit in relation to its Reserves held by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation and Temasek depends on the long-term expected returns on those assets.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is not based on actual cash contributions of the entities to the Government.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: She mentioned whether any KOM staff will be prosecuted depends on whether they benefited from this scam.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One, would the Senior Minister of State clarify whether bonuses and salary increases given to senior staff, past and present, for meeting profit and revenue targets are deemed as personal benefits?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Second, the Senior Minister of State also mentioned that the corruption is done outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify whether the email trail leads back to senior staff in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the investigation of the scam, did the email trail lead back to Singapore, which means were senior staff in Singapore actually orchestrating or sanctioning all these from Singapore?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is not a single factor; it is a whole array of factors which the Public Prosecutor will have to take into account.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second question was – could the Member just repeat the second question, that the corruption was done outside Singapore and therefore—?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify whether the email trail leads back to senior staff in Singapore, as in whether approval or directions were given by senior staff from Singapore?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All these are matters which are subject to investigation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I do not have this information and it certainly would not be appropriate for me to enquire on this point.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is something which the Public Prosecutor and CPIB are looking into.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Let proper process, due process take place and, in time, they will have to make the appropriate decision.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: There was a third supplementary question on clawing back illegal payouts and thus, whether the Government would order a forensic audit since this is one of the biggest corruption scandals in corporate Singapore?
